timeline.title: Born Ma He
timeline.text: Zheng He was born Ma He in 1371 in Kunyang, near Kunming, to a Hui Muslim family. His father's name, Ma Hajji, shows that a forebear had made the pilgrimage to Mecca.

timeline.title: Captured as a boy
timeline.text: In 1381 Ming armies conquered Yunnan, and his father died during the conquest. The boy was captured and, as happened to many captives, made a eunuch. He was sent to serve Zhu Di, the Prince of Yan, in the north.

timeline.title: Civil war
timeline.text: When Zhu Di rebelled against his nephew, the Jianwen Emperor, Ma He fought on his side in the Jingnan campaign of 1399 to 1402.

timeline.title: His master becomes emperor
timeline.text: Zhu Di won the war and took the throne as the Yongle Emperor. His trusted servant rose with him.

timeline.title: A new name: Zheng
timeline.text: In 1404 the emperor gave him the surname Zheng. From then on he was known as Zheng He, a senior palace official.

timeline.title: The first voyage
timeline.text: An edict of 11 July 1405 launched the first voyage. Records give 62 treasure ships and about 27,800 men; a total of 317 ships is often given but is uncertain. The fleet sailed to Champa, Java, Malacca, Sumatra, Ceylon and Calicut on the coast of India.

timeline.title: The pirate fleet
timeline.text: On the way home, the fleet defeated the pirate fleet of Chen Zuyi at Palembang. Chen was taken to China and executed. The fleet returned to Nanjing on 2 October 1407.

timeline.title: Straight out again
timeline.text: A second voyage was ordered at once and sailed to Siam, Java, Sumatra and the Indian coast, returning in 1409. Historians debate whether Zheng He himself sailed on it.

timeline.title: A stone in three languages
timeline.text: A tablet dated 15 February 1409, in Chinese, Tamil and Persian, records gifts from the fleet to the Buddha, to a Hindu god and to Allah. It was found in Galle in 1911 and is now in the Colombo National Museum.

timeline.title: Fighting in Ceylon
timeline.text: On the third voyage (1409 to 1411), Zheng He's troops fought King Alakeshvara of Kotte, took his capital and carried him to China. The emperor later released the captives.

timeline.title: Beyond India
timeline.text: The fourth voyage sailed in December 1413 and went further than ever: past Calicut to the Maldives and to Hormuz at the mouth of the Persian Gulf. The interpreter Ma Huan, who later wrote a book about the lands he saw, joined the fleet.

timeline.title: Home from Hormuz
timeline.text: After defeating a rival ruler, Sekandar, in northern Sumatra, the fleet returned to Nanjing on 12 August 1415.

timeline.title: To Africa
timeline.text: The fifth voyage (1417 to 1419) carried foreign envoys home and reached Aden in Arabia and Mogadishu, Brava and Malindi in East Africa. Fleets of this time brought back exotic animals, including a giraffe.

timeline.title: The sixth voyage
timeline.text: The sixth voyage escorted envoys of 16 states home. The fleet split into squadrons, one reaching Aden. A 2002 book claimed that his fleets reached America this year; historians reject this as pseudohistory.

timeline.title: Lightning at the palace
timeline.text: In May 1421 lightning struck the emperor's new palace in Beijing. Some at court saw it as a sign against the voyages, and further voyages were suspended.

timeline.title: The voyages stop
timeline.text: The Yongle Emperor died in 1424. The new Hongxi Emperor ended the voyages that September. Zheng He and his men served as the garrison of Nanjing.

timeline.title: One more voyage
timeline.text: The Xuande Emperor ordered a seventh voyage on 29 June 1430. The fleet left Nanjing on 19 January 1431.

timeline.title: The Liujiagang stone
timeline.text: Waiting to sail, Zheng He and his fellow envoys set up an inscription at the temple of the sea goddess Tianfei, recording their voyages and thanking her for protection.

timeline.title: The Changle stone
timeline.text: A second inscription, at Changle, lists seven voyages since 1405, more than thirty countries and more than one hundred thousand li of sea. It is the best summary of the voyages in his own officers' words.

timeline.title: The last voyage
timeline.text: The seventh fleet called at Champa, Java, Palembang, Malacca, Sumatra, Ceylon, Calicut and Hormuz. A squadron under Hong Bao visited Bengal and, according to an inscription, sent men to Mecca.

timeline.title: Death of Zheng He
timeline.text: Zheng He probably died during or soon after the last voyage, in 1433 or 1435; accounts differ. One account says he was buried at sea off the Malabar Coast. His tomb in Nanjing is a memorial without his body.

timeline.title: Ma Huan's book
timeline.text: Ma Huan's Yingya Shenglan, an account of the countries he visited with the fleet, was published. With books by Fei Xin and Gong Zhen, it is a key source for the voyages. Most official records of the voyages were later lost.

timeline.title: Remembered again
timeline.text: Official Ming histories played the voyages down. Interest returned after the writer Liang Qichao published a biography of Zheng He in 1904.

timeline.title: Maritime Day
timeline.text: In 2005, 600 years after the first voyage, China began marking 11 July, the date of the first voyage's edict, as Maritime Day. The true size of his largest ships is still debated: legends claim about 127 metres, while many scholars suggest 60 to 75 metres.

feature.title: The seven voyages
feature.lead: Between 1405 and 1433 Zheng He led seven great fleets from China into the Indian Ocean. Each voyage reached further, from the spice ports of Southeast Asia to Arabia and East Africa.

items.label: First voyage
items.text: Dozens of treasure ships and about 27,800 men sailed to the pepper port of Calicut in India. On the way home they defeated the pirate Chen Zuyi at Palembang.

items.label: Second voyage
items.text: Envoys were carried home and a dispute with Java was settled. Whether Zheng He sailed himself is debated.

items.label: Third voyage
items.text: The fleet left a stone in three languages at Galle and fought the king of Kotte in Sri Lanka, taking him to China.

items.label: Fourth voyage
items.text: The first voyage beyond India, reaching Hormuz in the Persian Gulf. The interpreter Ma Huan sailed with the fleet.

items.label: Fifth voyage
items.text: The fleet reached Arabia and the East African coast, carrying envoys home and bringing back exotic animals.

items.label: Sixth voyage
items.place: Sumatra, Ceylon, Hormuz, Aden, East Africa
items.text: Envoys of 16 states were escorted home, with squadrons sent to different ports. Claims that a fleet reached America are rejected by historians.

items.label: The pause
items.text: A new emperor ended the voyages. The fleet's men became the garrison of Nanjing.

items.label: The stones of 1431
items.text: Before the last voyage, Zheng He and his officers carved the story of all their voyages in two inscriptions to the sea goddess.

items.label: Seventh voyage
items.text: The last great fleet. A squadron reached Bengal and sent men toward Mecca. Zheng He probably died on or soon after this voyage.

works.title: The seven treasure voyages
works.text: Seven fleet voyages from 1405 to 1433 that linked Ming China with Southeast Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa through trade, gifts and diplomacy, and sometimes force.

works.title: Commanding the fleet
works.text: Organising dozens of large treasure ships and tens of thousands of sailors, soldiers and officials on round trips of two years or more.

works.title: Defeat of the pirate Chen Zuyi
works.text: The fleet broke a pirate force at Palembang that threatened shipping in the Strait of Malacca.

works.title: Galle Trilingual Inscription
works.text: A stone tablet in Chinese, Tamil and Persian offering gifts to the Buddha, a Hindu god and Allah. Now in the Colombo National Museum.

works.title: Envoys from many lands
works.text: The fleets carried foreign envoys to China and home again, sometimes envoys of 16 states at once.

works.title: The routes of the Mao Kun map
works.text: A sailing chart from Nanjing to Hormuz and East Africa, preserved in a book of 1628 and thought to date from about 1422. Its maker is unknown.

works.title: Liujiagang inscription
works.text: A stone at the sea goddess's temple in Liujiagang, recording the voyages and the fleet's thanks for safe passage.

works.title: Changle inscription
works.text: A stone at Changle summing up seven voyages, more than thirty countries and their main ports, in Zheng He's officers' own words.

books.author: W. W. Rockhill
books.note: Published in parts in T'oung Pao (1914-1915), based on Chinese records of the ports and peoples the fleets visited. Zheng He left no book of his own.
